doc.title: Keter Betts interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 11, 1996

title: Shakespeare and music as a human constant
summary: He cites the Merchant of Venice on those without music and says archaeologists always find art, dance and music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Well that was at the time. And it just showed you that, like I said how powerful music is. Because if you check out Shakespeare, if I can remember what it was, Shakespeare, talking to the daughter in “The Merchant of Venice,” and you’ll find a part in there, I’m trying to figure what chapter it is, but he’s telling his daughter he says, “pity the poor man who has no music within his soul, for this person is guilty of treason.” And he goes on to elaborate about the person who has no music within him. And you check that out. You’ll find it most interesting. And I use this at times when I’m at conferences or something, about being wary about people who really don’t have a deep feeling within themselves for music because they are like Shakespeare says, guilty of treason. And it’s treason against music. And when archeologists, if you look in the last three, four, five © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-

hundred years whenever archeologists, wherever they go and they find they discover ruins from the most primitive tribes to the most sophisticated and advanced, they always find some form of art, dance and music, which means that the human being has always entertained themselves, from the very beginning.
And that’s the things that we leave for the next generations.

All the generations to come. Because you still want to do something with your hands. He’s doing something with his hands. He could have it automatically, even if he just sits there and doesn’t touch it. But he wants to be a part of it.
